title: Portal audit log
description: Who did what, when (portal plan P5.3; D456, D457, F9). The log is append-only and the portal writes no endpoint that edits or deletes one: an entry that could be changed after the fact would not answer the question the log exists for. Reads are entries too (D456) — an operations member reading a customer's metadata is a fact about that customer — so a burst of reads is visible in the same list as a key's revocation. Every object here is closed, because ee/keyservice/wire_audit.go decodes it with DisallowUnknownFields.

entry.description: One line of the audit log.

id.description: The entry's id, and the only handle it has: nothing else in the portal points at an audit line, so an entry cannot be linked to from something that could later be edited.

at.description: When the act happened, in UTC, from the server's clock and not the request's: the sign-in freshness rule is measured against this service's own time (D2187), so a client's idea of now is not evidence.

actor_uid.description: The Firebase uid of whoever acted. The uid is the identity and the email below is what a person reads, kept separately because an email can be reassigned inside a workspace and a uid cannot.

actor_email.description: The email the actor signed in with, as it was at the time. It is copied into the entry rather than looked up later: the log has to say what was true then, and a member's email can change.

organisation_id.description: The organisation the act was in, or null for one that was not in one — a sign-in that created the first organisation, or an operations act that is the team's own.

action.description: What was done, as a short name the portal itself wrote. It is a name and not a sentence: the reader is a person with the spec open, and a translated sentence in a log is a sentence that changes meaning when the translation is edited.

target_id.description: What it was done to — the workspace, entitlement, invite or member — or null for an act with no single target. It is an id and not a copy of the object, because the object will change and the log has to say what was touched rather than what it looked like.

read.description: True for an entry that records reading rather than changing (D456). It is a flag and not a separate log, so reads sit in the same list as writes and can be counted against a person in one query.

detail.description: The little that is worth keeping beside the action — a reason operations gave, or the previous value a change replaced — or null when the action speaks for itself. It never carries a key or a renewal secret: F5 holds for the log as it does everywhere else, and an audit line is read by more people than a key is.
